name: Amira Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for doing this, Amira. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Brightline Catering Supply. We sell to hotels, canteens and cafés, so I'm buying takeaway cups, napkins, gloves, cleaning chemicals, foil trays, all the boring things nobody notices until they run out. Most of the day I'm on the phone or email with about thirty suppliers, checking stock levels in our system and placing orders. I keep a paper notebook of every supplier's quirks, like which one always ships short on a Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy knowing my suppliers. When there was a glove shortage two years ago, I got us stock because a sales rep I'd known for years picked up the phone for me. What drains me is the new reorder software the company keeps pushing. It suggests orders that make no sense, so I do them my own way and then get asked why I ignored it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I'd like, honestly. That's sort of what I already think is going on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I told you so, nicely. To friends I'd say all that noise and we're still ordering cups the same way. I don't post online much, maybe a comment on a cousin's post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I can keep doing my job the way I'm good at it. I'm paid well for a buyer, I've got over a year's money put away, and Brightline isn't going anywhere. The reorder software might get a bit better and do the dull top-ups, which I could live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, maybe let the software do the toilet roll and bin bag reorders since those never change. I'd keep putting money aside each month toward a flat deposit with Tomás, my partner. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, even. Like a storm forecast that turned out to be drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the software might take the dull top-ups. Would that change your days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Maybe an hour a day less on repeat orders. I'd fill it with supplier calls, which is the part I'm good at anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else on your mind for the next few years, even with AI stalling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the flat. Prices keep going up and Tomás and I want to buy before we think about anything else. If AI flopped, buying a flat with my partner would still be the thing I lie awake about, not my job.

say: I'd tell colleagues, nicely, that **I told them so**.
I'd say to friends we're still **ordering cups** the same old way.
think: I keep doing the job the way **I'm good** at it.
Good pay, **a year's savings** and a stable firm mean my job feels secure.
do: Keep buying as I do, letting the software handle **repeat top-ups**.
Keep saving monthly toward a **flat deposit** with Tomás.
feel: **Calm** and relieved, like a storm that turned out to be **drizzle**.
S0.quote: If AI flopped, buying a flat with my partner would still be the thing I lie awake about, not my job.
fieldNote: Amira already **distrusts the reorder software** and quietly works around it.
Her real pressure is **housing**, not work, and she says so plainly.
She values **supplier relationships** above any tool, citing the glove shortage.

steps.text: Let the reorder software handle bin bag and toilet roll top-ups
Keep putting a set amount aside monthly for the flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying. You actually said buying. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the computer can't phone a rep at seven in the evening and get you a pallet of gloves. To friends I'd be more worried, I'd say they're coming for office jobs like mine first. I wouldn't post anything, it'd only end up being read by my boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Brightline would cut the buying team from five to two or three and give the rest of the job to that software. I don't use AI and I've been slow on the software, so I'm not the one they'd keep. I've got savings and there are lots of distributors around here, but they'd all be doing the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop spending on the extras and add another few hundred a month to savings. I'd look for a buyer job at a smaller family-run supplier that's slow to change, there are a few near the ring road. I wouldn't jump straight away though, I'd wait a few months and see who Brightline actually lets go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight feeling in my chest. I've always been the one who's good at buying, and suddenly being good at it doesn't count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI. Would you try learning it, given all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I tried one of those chat things once to write a supplier email and it made up a delivery date. I'd rather move somewhere that still needs people who know the phone numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, oddly. He was a lorry driver for twenty years and he saw the routes go onto computers. He'd tell me to keep my head down and keep my savings close.

say: At work I'd say software **can't phone a rep** at seven in the evening.
To friends I'd admit **office jobs** like mine are first in line.
think: I expect Brightline to cut the **five buyers** to two or three.
As someone **slow on software**, I don't think I'd be one of those kept.
do: Cut extras and add **a few hundred** a month to savings.
Look for a buyer job at a **family-run supplier** slow to change.
Wait **a few months** to see who Brightline lets go.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight chest, because being good at buying may **stop counting**.
S1.quote: I've always been the one who's good at buying, and suddenly being good at it doesn't count.
fieldNote: Amira places herself among the **likely cuts** because she avoids the tools.
She chooses to **move rather than learn**, citing one bad experience with a chatbot.
Her dad's experience as a **lorry driver** shapes her keep-your-head-down instinct.

steps.text: Add a few hundred more a month to the savings account
Apply for buyer jobs at family-run suppliers near the ring road
Wait a few months to see who Brightline lets go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not a change, that's my job just ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say someone needs to tell us what the plan is, because a lot of people here have mortgages. To friends I'd say the government had better have something ready. I'd probably go quiet online, it's too depressing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out of a job in eighteen months, maybe less. Every buying job around here would go at the same time, so having plenty of jobs nearby wouldn't help. The warehouse lads would get three more years before the robots come, and I'd be jealous of them, which is a strange thing to feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the flat on hold straight away and keep the deposit as my safety money. Tomás and I would cut back hard: no holiday, no new car, cooking at home. I'd ask the warehouse manager about moving onto the floor, forklift or goods-in checking, because at least that's three more years. And I'd lean on my parents if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. I'm twenty-seven and I'd have spent five years getting good at buying, something that just stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move to the warehouse floor. How would that feel, going from buyer to goods-in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Humbling. Probably less pay, maybe a third less. But my dad drove lorries and he was proud of it, so I'd get over myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the flat's off for now. He works in hotel maintenance, so he's hands-on, and he'd probably be fine longer than me. That'd be a strange switch, me depending on his wage.

say: I'd ask management for **a clear plan**, because colleagues have mortgages.
I'd tell friends the **government** had better have something ready.
think: I expect to be **out of work** within about eighteen months.
Plenty of local jobs won't help when **every buying job** goes together.
do: Put the **flat purchase** on hold and keep the deposit as safety money.
Cut holidays and a **new car**, and cook at home.
Ask about a **goods-in role** on the warehouse floor for three extra years.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless, watching five years of skill **just stop**.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven and I'd have spent five years getting good at buying, something that just stops.
fieldNote: Amira expects **certain job loss** and notices local job numbers won't protect her.
She'd take a **pay cut** of about a third to buy time on the warehouse floor.
She notes the reversal of **relying on her partner**, who does hands-on hotel work.

steps.text: Pause the flat purchase and keep the deposit as emergency money
Drop the holiday and new car and cook at home
Ask the warehouse manager for a goods-in or forklift role
Lean on parents for help if the job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So 2031 for my kind of work. That's still soon, but it's not next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we've got time, let's not lose our heads. To friends I'd say I'm going to have to do something, I just don't know what yet. Still nothing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, buying is still finished, it just takes five years. I'm not going to become someone who loves computers, that's not me. But five years is enough to get a qualification in something you do with your hands or face to face, and robots for that come in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at an evening course, maybe health and safety or hospitality management, something where I'm with people. I'd still buy the flat, maybe a smaller one, because Tomás's work looks steadier. And I'd put a bit extra aside every month just in case it's quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still. It's like knowing the date your lease ends and not having found anywhere yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't become someone who loves computers. Not even a little, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe enough to not get laughed at, fine. But I'm not going to make my living off it. I'd rather learn something where they still need a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hospitality management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know the customers, I sell to them every day. Hotel managers ring me in a panic about napkins for a wedding, and somebody still has to stand in that ballroom and sort it out.

say: I'd tell colleagues we **have time** and shouldn't panic.
I'd admit to friends I **must change** something but don't know what.
think: Buying is **still finished**; it just takes five years.
Five years is enough for a **face-to-face qualification**, with robots not until 2034.
do: Start an **evening course** in health and safety or hospitality management.
Still buy a **smaller flat**, since my partner's work looks steadier.
Put **a bit extra** aside each month in case it's faster.
feel: Still **anxious**, like knowing your **lease ends** with nowhere lined up.
S3.quote: Hotel managers ring me in a panic about napkins for a wedding, and somebody still has to stand in that ballroom and sort it out.
fieldNote: Five years doesn't change her verdict, only gives **time to retrain**.
She steers away from AI toward **face-to-face work** like hospitality management.
Her partner's **hands-on job** makes her feel safe enough to still buy a flat.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening hospitality management course this autumn
Buy a smaller flat with Tomás on his steadier wage
Save an extra amount each month as a buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a lot of time. Easy to waste it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a long way off and things change. To friends I'd say it sounds like something I'll deal with in my thirties. Nothing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be tempted to ignore it for five years, and I know that's stupid. Buying ends in 2036 and I'd be thirty-seven. That's an awkward age to start again, but not impossible, and I'd have savings by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep buying for now, and keep saving. I'd tell myself I'll start retraining in year three or four, once it's clearer what work's left. We'd buy the flat as planned and maybe think about kids, because ten years is enough for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quieter. It's in the back of my mind instead of in my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until year three or four. What would make you start earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Brightline started cutting buyers early. Or if a buyer left and nobody was hired. If Brightline stopped replacing buyers who leave, that's when I'd know the AI change is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would kids look like, knowing this was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want them. My grandparents had kids through worse. But I'd want one of us in a job that lasts past 2039, so probably Tomás.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long way off and things change.
I'd tell friends it's something for **my thirties**.
think: I'd be tempted to **ignore it** for five years, and I know that's stupid.
Buying ends when I'm **thirty-seven**, awkward but not impossible.
do: Keep buying and **keep saving** for now.
Plan to start **retraining** in year three or four.
Buy the flat and **think about kids** within the ten years.
feel: Still **anxious**, but quieter, sitting at the **back** of my mind.
S4.quote: If Brightline stopped replacing buyers who leave, that's when I'd know the AI change is real.
fieldNote: Amira openly predicts her own **delay**, which she calls stupid.
Her trigger to act is concrete: **buyers not replaced** at Brightline.
She plans **children** and relies on her partner's longer-lasting hands-on job.

steps.text: Keep buying at Brightline and saving the same monthly amount
Wait until buyers stop being replaced before retraining
Buy the flat and plan for a first child with Tomás

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I wouldn't be ready and nobody else would be either. What would help is someone actually helping you move sideways into another job, like proper placements, not just a website with courses on it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me want to change at all. Everyone assumes you should just learn the new thing, but some of us were good at the old thing and we'd like that to count.

headlineQuote: Everyone assumes you should just learn the new thing, but some of us were good at the old thing and we'd like that to count.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old buyer** of catering supplies who knows her suppliers by phone.
She **never uses AI** and quietly works around Brightline's reorder software.
With **strong savings**, her main worry outside AI is buying a flat with Tomás.
She feels **anxious or alarmed** in every change scenario, expecting to be among the first cut.
She prefers moving to **face-to-face or hands-on work** over learning the tools.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because neither she nor anyone else would be ready.
whatWouldHelp: Real **job placements** that move people sideways, not just a website of courses.
